While presenting at the National Speakers Association (NSA) Convention in Orlando, I was able to hear dozens of presentations and speeches.  The experience led me to think about what makes a presentation or speech effective, which I define as the ability to communicate your message clearly in a way that is meaningful to the audience.
Here are the 10 factors that can make you effective when you present or speak:
1.	You know your subject.
It's obvious to me and the rest of the audience that you know your material well and can handle questions with ease.  You are confident but not cocky. It's okay if you use notes, but you are not buried in them.
2.	You communicate a clear message.
Not only do you know your subject well, but you are able to focus it into a concise message that I can understand, regardless of my level of expertise.
3.	Your message is relevant to me (also known as "you care about the audience").
You explain how your message relates to me and my experience.  Once I heard someone give a speech that consisted entirely of stories about his experiences with famous people, to which I couldn't relate at all.  I kept thinking, "how does this help ME?"
4.	You are prepared.
You show your respect for me and the rest of the audience by moving through your points in an organized manner, speaking within the time limit and comfortably handling the room environment and logistics.
5.	You keep my attention.
You vary your voice and body language so you are interesting to listen to and watch.  You make eye contact with me, you speak loudly enough so I can hear you easily and your body language matches your words.
6.	You care about your subject.
Your presentation or speech conveys your sincere enthusiasm for your subject.  You don't have to be jumping up and down in the front of the room, but if you don't care about your subject, why should I?
7.	You share stories and examples.
Your stories don't have to be long or overly dramatic; they can be short examples or anecdotes that illustrate your message and help it make sense to me.
8.	Your slides are not the focus.
You remember that you are the presentation and your slides are just the visual aids.  You spend most of your time making eye contact with the audience instead of looking at the screen.  Your slides are easy to read and contain high-quality images.  (Or, you don't use slides at all!)
9.	You are authentic.
You are your real self instead of putting on an act or pretending.  You connect with me and the rest of the audience by sharing your real experiences and opinions.  And you're the same person offstage as when you're onstage.
10.	 You're not perfect.
When something unexpected happens or you make a mistake, you acknowledge it with grace and humor.  And we are reminded that the goal is communication, not perfection, since perfection is unrealistic and unnecessary.
The next time you have to give a presentation or speech for any kind of audience, make sure you include these 10 factors, so you can be effective.

How to Be a Good Speaker: The Best 10 Tips
10 Easy Ways to Be a Good Speaker
No doubt, public speaking is an art in itself. But what if it isn’t a talent you were born with? Is it actually possible to learn how to be a good speaker and win it every time you take the floor? In this guide, we will go through 10 useful tips that will help you gain more confidence, show off your expertise in the subject and engage your audience regardless of the occasion.
10 Easy Ways to Be a Good Speaker
1
Work on your presenter personality
For a good public speaker, the first impression can make it or break it. From the choice of your clothes and shoes to the pace and pitch of your voice, everything is going to be closely analyzed by your audience. This is perfectly normal, since it is you who are in the limelight, while they could judge you from the comfort of their seats in the back. Remember to make appropriate choice and don’t try to embarrass anyone unless it is intentional.
2
Learn from top public speakers
You can’t learn how to be a good speaker by reading motivational books only. Instead, turn to the masters of this art, someone who is or was famous for striking the perfect chemistry with the audience. One of the options is stand-up comedians and TED presenters – all of them know how to deliver on the subject while keeping the audience entertained. While it’s not easy at all, you could steal from them some useful techniques – your body language, pace of speech, use of pauses, and so on, which could help you become truly a rock star of public speaking.
3
Practice, practice, practice
There is never too much rehearsing, and practice does make perfect. Don’t be afraid of losing the interest in your subject before you actually present it – the more you repeat your speech, the more you grow into it, starting to feel all the weaknesses and strengths of it. Rehearsing in front of your friends or unknown people helps a lot, so don’t miss a chance to ask them to sit for you as you speak. Also, ask for honest feedback afterwards.
4
Think of the audience as your friends
It won’t help you to grasp how to be a good speaker if you keep thinking that you are going into a lion’s cage. Instead, quiet your mind and address them amicably, as all of you are here to accomplish a common goal (be it learning new information or coming up with a solution to some problem). You can’t possibly guess how nerve-wrecking it was for me as a twenty-something student to pitch a business plan to a panel of internationally renowned bankers. Yet, I survived. How? I knew they wished me well, and I drew them to participation since we were there for the same mission.
5
Get your props
When delivering a public speech, it should not be only about you talking. Treat your audience to superb visuals and audio materials, where appropriate, to reinforce your ideas and provide additional evidence in support of your point. Just remember not to overdo it – if you make a presentation, your slides should contain no more than 20% of text, while bringing up relevant, sometimes humorous pictures increases the chances that the facts you emphasize will be remembered afterwards.
6
Start with a perfect lead
You would want your audience to relax and become your friends right off from the start. For this, your introduction should be as compelling as possible, so always try to come up with a perfect hook such as a relevant joke, a weird occurrence from the past or a funny fact that would show you have both a sense of humor and mercy not to bore your listeners to death.
7
Leave room for improvisation
When preparing for your public appearance, remember that it’s not about impeccable memorizing of everything you or someone else wrote down. A critical part of this art is knowing the ideas rather than just the fancy combinations of words. Practice until you can easily navigate the space of your speech remembering only the hallmarks, so that you could improvise and deviate from the subject without losing your point.
8
Be personal
Share your emotional side and draw the audience into your world by mentioning some personal facts to which they could relate. Again, it would show you are not just some nerd who knows the subject so well they invited you to speak on it. Prove that you are not only a good expert but also a human who skyrocketed to that level of expertise by trials and errors, as the art of how to be a good speaker is also about being able to read your audience and guess what can be most engaging for them to hear.
9
Interact with the audience
It’s important to engage your audience into your presentation as well, so that they won’t feel alienated. Many of your listeners would have something to contribute to your story, and sometimes it can turn out to ease the atmosphere. There’ll definitely be some awkward situations, but dealing with them is part of the public speaking art as well. Also, you are bound to have a good laugh too, it’s always so entertaining.
10
End on a high note
I know it’s so stressful to make up a perfect conclusion to your speech, but you should leave your audience with both food for thought and a sense of accomplishment. Don’t be afraid to leave it hanging in the air either, for example, for asking an open question for them to think about. Other than this, wrapping up your speech with a neat summary would work for corporate presentations as much as for more general subjects. Just make sure the conclusion won’t take more than 5% of the total time.
